1	\section{Experiments}
2	
3	\subsection{Death Avoidance Decomposition}
4	\label{sec:death-decomp}
5	
6	\begin{figure}[t]
7	\centering
8	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig1_daf_scatter.pdf}
9	\caption{Per-task scatter plot: death rate differential (internal minus deterministic) vs.\ performance gap ($\Delta_{\text{full}}$). Pearson $r = 0.9698$ ($p = 8.12 \times 10^{-7}$). Each point is one of 11 ScienceWorld task types.}
10	\label{fig:decomposition}
11	\end{figure}
12	
13	The full performance gap between deterministic and internal strategies across 245 episodes is $\Delta_{\text{full}} = +29.60$ points. When we exclude all episodes where either strategy results in agent death, the gap collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$. The resulting Death Avoidance Factor (\S\ref{sec:daf}) is 90.41\%: approximately 90\% of the deterministic strategy's advantage over internal reasoning is attributable to death avoidance rather than superior task performance when both agents survive.
14	
15	This concentration is consistent across task types (Appendix~\ref{app:per-task}). The Pearson correlation between per-task death rate differential and $\Delta_{\text{full}}$ is $r = 0.9698$ ($p = 8.12 \times 10^{-7}$; bootstrap 95\% CI $[0.952, 0.995]$), as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:decomposition}. Spearman rank correlation is $\rho = 0.986$ ($p = 2.4 \times 10^{-8}$), and leave-one-out analysis shows $r \in [0.963, 0.980]$---no single task type is a leverage point (Appendix~\ref{app:correlation}). We note that death rate differential and $\Delta_{\text{full}}$ are structurally coupled through the penalty term $P$, so high correlation is expected when death dominates. The empirically non-trivial finding is that 78.9\% of non-tie routing labels are driven by death asymmetry independent of $P$. Knowing how much more frequently the internal strategy dies is nearly sufficient to predict the full performance gap for a given task type. The internal strategy dies in 42.9\% of episodes compared to 16.3\% for deterministic computation---a 2.6$\times$ ratio that drives the bulk of the observed score difference.
16	
17	The episode-level label distribution reflects this asymmetry: of 245 episodes, 86 are \texttt{det\_preferred}, only 9 \texttt{internal\_preferred}, and 150 \texttt{no\_preference}---when internal reasoning does not cause death, it performs comparably to deterministic computation.
18	
19	Notably, the per-task DAF distribution is bimodal: \texttt{find-non-living-thing} exhibits DAF $\approx 0\%$ (routing signal entirely from non-death score differences, $\Delta = +9.58$), while all other task types exceed 85\%.
20	
21	One task reveals the residual non-death signal. \texttt{find-non-living-thing} ($n=40$) has zero deaths under both strategies yet shows $\Delta_{\text{full}} = +9.58$, entirely from non-death performance differences---deterministic computation can provide advantages through more accurate state tracking even when agents survive. However, among the 10 death-prone task types, death avoidance overwhelms non-death differences. When both modalities survive, the gap is small but non-negligible ($\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$, 9.6\% of $\Delta_{\text{full}}$).
22	
23	\subsection{Baselines}
24	\label{sec:baselines}
25	
26	\begin{table}[t]
27	\centering
28	\small
29	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
30	\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
31	\toprule
32	Strategy & Score & 95\% CI & Death \% \\
33	\midrule
34	Always-Internal & $-39.07$ & [$-46.40$, $-32.27$] & 42.9 \\
35	Always-Deterministic & $-9.47$ & [$-14.71$, $-4.29$] & 16.3 \\
36	Random & $-22.38$ & [$-28.67$, $-15.75$] & 27.8 \\
37	Oracle & $-6.58$ & [$-11.54$, $-1.70$] & 14.3 \\
38	\midrule
39	Trained Router$^\dagger$ & $-10.70$ & [$-16.33$, $-5.27$] & 17.6 \\
40	\bottomrule
41	\end{tabular}}
42	\caption{Episode-weighted mean scores on ScienceWorld (11 task types, 245 episodes). 95\% Bootstrap CIs. The oracle selects the higher-scoring strategy per episode; 96.3\% of its decisions match the always-deterministic strategy. $\dagger$\,4-seed mean.}
43	\label{tab:baselines}
44	\end{table}
45	
46	Table~\ref{tab:baselines} reports episode-weighted mean scores and death rates for four unconditional strategies. Always-deterministic ($-9.47$) outperforms always-internal ($-39.07$) by 29.60 points, consistent with $\Delta_{\text{full}}$. The oracle, which selects the higher-scoring strategy per episode, improves only modestly to $-6.58$, with 96.3\% of its routing decisions matching always-deterministic. This \emph{oracle degeneracy} indicates that the optimal episode-level routing policy closely resembles unconditional deterministic computation---the routing signal is insufficient to improve upon simply always choosing the deterministic strategy. Random routing ($-22.38$) falls between the two pure strategies, with a death rate (27.8\%) proportional to its 50/50 allocation.
47	
48	Keyword-based routing fails structurally: match rates cluster at extremes (85.8\% or $<$5\%), precluding meaningful routing discrimination.
49	
50	\subsection{Router Training as Diagnostic}
51	\label{sec:router-diagnostic}
52	
53	A natural question is whether the episode-level counterfactual labels can train a step-level router. We investigate this as a diagnostic probe of label informativeness rather than a routing system proposal, testing two architectures.
54	
55	\paragraph{Classification head.} A linear head on LLM hidden representations, trained on episode-level labels, degenerates to always-deterministic (0\% internal recall) across all configurations (class weighting, focal loss, undersampling, temperature scaling).
56	
57	\paragraph{Implicit router.} We fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B to internalize routing decisions within its generation (Appendix~\ref{app:router-details}). Across four seeds, balanced accuracy is $58.1 \pm 0.8\%$---above chance but insufficient for practical routing, with seed-level variation (Appendix~\ref{app:router-details}) reflecting threshold sensitivity rather than genuine signal.
58	
59	\paragraph{End-to-end evaluation.} Deployed as an episode-level router (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}), the trained router scores $-10.70$ (95\% CI $[-16.33, -5.27]$), not statistically outperforming always-deterministic ($-9.47$, $[-14.71, -4.29]$; overlapping CIs). The episode-to-step granularity mismatch is the bottleneck: when DAF $\approx 90\%$, router headroom is limited to the ${\sim}10\%$ non-death signal.
60	
61	\paragraph{Data split.} Of 245 episodes, 95 non-tie labels are split 85/15 (81 train, 14 validation; 1734/306 steps). Baselines in Table~\ref{tab:baselines} report trajectory statistics; the router score ($-10.70$) comes from fresh environment interaction.
62	
63	\paragraph{Labeling quality.} We verify label quality in Appendix~\ref{app:labeling}.
64	
65	\subsection{Cross-Model Verification}
66	\label{sec:cross-model}
67	
68	To test whether the death avoidance pattern is model-specific, we run a mechanism verification pilot with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on two task types (\texttt{freeze} and \texttt{find-non-living-thing}, 5 episode pairs each, $N{=}10$). Llama-8B achieves lower absolute ScienceWorld scores than Qwen-2.5-7B, reflecting weaker task-level capability, but the death pattern direction is consistent across model families.
69	
70	On \texttt{freeze}, the internal strategy dies in 40\% of episodes versus 20\% for deterministic (Qwen: 55\%/25\%)---the same directional asymmetry. The single non-tie episode arises from death asymmetry: the internal strategy dies while deterministic survives, producing a det-preferred label consistent with the Qwen pattern. On \texttt{find-non-living-thing}, both strategies achieve 0\% death rate under Llama, matching Qwen exactly; the 3 det-preferred labels arise from non-death score differences.
71	
72	\begin{table}[t]
73	\centering
74	\small
75	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
76	\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}
77	\toprule
78	Task & Model & D\%\textsubscript{int} & D\%\textsubscript{det} & $\Delta$D\% & D / I / N \\
79	\midrule
80	freeze & Qwen-7B & 55 & 25 & +30 & 6 / 0 / 14 \\
81	freeze & Llama-8B & 40 & 20 & +20 & 1 / 0 / 4 \\
82	\midrule
83	find-non-living & Qwen-7B & 0 & 0 & 0 & 16 / 4 / 20 \\
84	find-non-living & Llama-8B & 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 / 1 / 1 \\
85	\bottomrule
86	\end{tabular}}
87	\caption{Cross-model death rate comparison. Llama pilot: $n{=}5$ episodes per task; Qwen: from Table~\ref{tab:per-task}. $\Delta$D\%: internal minus deterministic death rate. D/I/N: det-preferred / internal-preferred / no-preference labels.}
88	\label{tab:cross-model}
89	\end{table}
90	
91	Table~\ref{tab:cross-model} summarizes the comparison. This pilot ($N{=}10$ episode pairs) provides preliminary directional evidence only: the sample size precludes statistical claims. Nevertheless, observing the same death asymmetry direction in a different model family (Llama vs.\ Qwen) suggests that the pattern reflects a structural property of internal reasoning in interactive environments rather than a model-specific artifact.

\section{Introduction}

Large language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.
A Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct agent navigating ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022}---a text-based science simulation with 30 task types---faces this choice at every step. Tracking temperature thresholds, container states, and multi-step procedures via internal reasoning is error-prone: the model may hallucinate that water has boiled when the stove was never activated, or that an object has been moved when the action was invalid. Deterministic external computation (environment simulators, code interpreters) eliminates such hallucinations via exact state transitions. The practical question for agent design is therefore: \emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus reasoning internally?}

Existing routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision.
Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} teaches models to insert API calls when doing so reduces perplexity; ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} selects among heterogeneous modules (search, code, vision) per subtask.
More recent adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \cite{mtrouter-2026}.
The shared assumption is that routing signal stems from diverse sources---accuracy, latency, capability matching---and that a learned router can exploit this signal to improve over any fixed strategy.
But this assumption has never been systematically verified: \emph{what actually drives the value of routing decisions in interactive environments?}

We find a surprisingly concentrated answer: \textbf{death avoidance accounts for approximately 90\% of the routing signal} in ScienceWorld.
The internal strategy's hallucination-induced failures trigger catastrophic agent death (a $-100$ penalty), while the deterministic strategy survives the same episodes.
Once death episodes are removed, the performance gap between strategies nearly vanishes.

Reaching this conclusion requires a methodological contribution.
The standard approach to generating routing labels---per-step oracle comparison---degenerates under sparse rewards.
In ScienceWorld, non-zero reward arrives only at episode termination; 97.4\% of steps (across 11 prescreened task types) produce identical scores regardless of modality, leaving no step-level signal to learn from (\S\ref{sec:collection}).
Keyword-based heuristics also fail structurally, as ScienceWorld actions lack science-specific terminology (\S\ref{sec:baselines}).
We instead propose \emph{episode-level counterfactual analysis}: run complete episodes under pure-internal (ReAct \cite{react-2023}) and pure-deterministic strategies, then compare episode outcomes to generate routing labels (\S\ref{sec:collection}).

Across 11 ScienceWorld task types (245 episode pairs), the full deterministic advantage is $\Delta_{\text{full}} = +29.60$ points.
Excluding death episodes, the gap collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$; 75 of 95 non-tie labels (78.9\%) arise from death asymmetry---a penalty-independent measure.
The penalty-sensitive Death Avoidance Factor (DAF; \S\ref{sec:daf}) is 90.41\% at the default penalty $P{=}100$, ranging from 46\% ($P{=}10$) to 95\% ($P{=}200$).
The per-task correlation between death-rate differential and performance gap is $r = 0.97$ ($p < 10^{-6}$, $n = 11$), confirming that death avoidance is the dominant mechanism across task types (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}).

Two cross-context checks probe the specificity of this finding.
First, a MATH Level~4--5 evaluation (300 problems), using a code interpreter as the deterministic modality, shows a directional reversal: internal reasoning outperforms code interpreter by $+4.3$ percentage points---the opposite direction from ScienceWorld.
In the absence of death risk, the deterministic advantage vanishes.
Second, a preliminary cross-model pilot with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ($N{=}10$ episode pairs, 2 task types) shows directionally consistent death patterns within ScienceWorld (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}), suggesting the phenomenon is not specific to a single model, though full-scale multi-model validation remains future work.
A trained router (Qwen3-1.7B with LoRA) achieves balanced accuracy of only ${\sim}58\%$, barely above chance, consistent with a signal so dominated by death avoidance that the residual learnable structure is thin (\S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Routing signal decomposition.}
    We identify step-level oracle degeneracy in sparse-reward environments and introduce episode-level counterfactual analysis with the DAF metric, a methodology for quantifying what fraction of routing signal derives from catastrophic-failure avoidance (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:daf}).

    \item \textbf{Death avoidance dominance.}
    On ScienceWorld, death asymmetry drives 78.9\% of non-tie routing labels independent of penalty magnitude (DAF = 90.41\% at $P{=}100$; $r = 0.97$ across task types), and a trained router does not significantly outperform always-deterministic (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}--\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

    \item \textbf{Cross-context validation.}
    On MATH ($N{=}300$), where death risk is absent, the routing signal reverses direction (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); a Llama-3.1-8B pilot within ScienceWorld shows consistent death-pattern direction (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}), providing evidence that the finding is driven by failure structure rather than model or domain specifics.

    \item \textbf{Router training as diagnostic probe.}
    Near-random balanced accuracy (${\sim}58\%$) of a trained router confirms that the learnable signal beyond death avoidance is structurally thin (\S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:method} describes the counterfactual collection procedure, episode-level labeling, and the DAF metric.
\S\ref{sec:death-decomp} presents the death avoidance decomposition and correlation analysis.
\S\ref{sec:baselines}--\ref{sec:cross-model} report baselines, router diagnostics, and cross-model verification.
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses cross-environment evidence and implications.

\subsection{Router Training as Diagnostic}
\label{sec:router-diagnostic}

A natural question is whether the episode-level counterfactual labels can train a step-level router. We investigate this as a diagnostic probe of label informativeness rather than a routing system proposal, testing two architectures.

\paragraph{Classification head.} A linear head on LLM hidden representations, trained on episode-level labels, degenerates to always-deterministic (0\% internal recall) across all configurations (class weighting, focal loss, undersampling, temperature scaling).

\paragraph{Implicit router.} We fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B to internalize routing decisions within its generation (Appendix~\ref{app:router-details}). Across four training seeds with a fixed data split, balanced accuracy is $57.6 \pm 0.5\%$; when the train/validation split is also varied, cross-split variance is substantially higher ($55.4 \pm 5.2\%$; Appendix~\ref{app:seed-robustness}), as the small validation set (14 episodes) amplifies split sensitivity. Both estimates are above chance but insufficient for practical routing.

\paragraph{End-to-end evaluation.} Deployed as an episode-level router (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}), the trained router scores $-10.70$ (95\% CI $[-16.33, -5.27]$), not statistically outperforming always-deterministic ($-9.47$, $[-14.71, -4.29]$; overlapping CIs). The episode-to-step granularity mismatch is the bottleneck: when DAF $\approx 90\%$, router headroom is limited to the ${\sim}10\%$ non-death signal.

\paragraph{Data split.} Of 245 episodes, 95 non-tie labels are split 85/15 (81 train, 14 validation; 1734/306 steps). Baselines in Table~\ref{tab:baselines} report trajectory statistics; the router score ($-10.70$) comes from fresh environment interaction.

\paragraph{Labeling quality.} We verify label quality in Appendix~\ref{app:labeling}.

Applied to 245 ScienceWorld episodes across 11 task types with a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone, this analysis reveals that death avoidance accounts for approximately 90\% of routing value (DAF $= 90.41\%$ at $P{=}100$; $\Delta_\text{full} = 29.60$ vs.\ $\Delta_\text{nd} = 2.84$), with 78.9\% of non-tie labels arising from death asymmetry alone and strong cross-task correlation ($r = 0.97$, $p < 10^{-6}$).
4

First, cross-environment analysis on MATH ($N{=}300$), where no death penalty exists, shows that the routing signal vanishes and directionally reverses: internal reasoning scores $+4.3$ percentage points higher than code execution ($81.0\%$ vs.\ $76.7\%$; CI $[0, 8.7]$, not significant), and the label distribution inverts from 86:9 deterministic-preferred in ScienceWorld to 30:17 internal-preferred. This contrast confirms that death avoidance, not an inherent advantage of deterministic computation, is the primary driver. Second, a Llama-3.1-8B pilot replicates the direction of the death differential (freeze death gap $+20\%$, consistent with Qwen's $+30\%$), providing preliminary evidence that the pattern generalizes across model families.
6	
7	A trained routing classifier achieves only 57--59\% balanced accuracy across four seeds, confirming that once death avoidance is accounted for, the remaining learnable signal is thin. The classification head variant degenerates to always-deterministic predictions despite achieving non-trivial logit-level separation, suggesting that discriminative routing over LLM representations is fundamentally limited in this regime.
8	
9	These results carry a practical implication: in environments with catastrophic failure modes, routing value is dominated by safety rather than efficiency. The router functions primarily as a safety critic---steering away from fatal actions---rather than as an optimizer selecting the more efficient strategy. System designers may therefore benefit from treating routing as a risk-management mechanism in such settings.
10	
11	Several directions remain open. Step-level counterfactual labeling could localize where within an episode routing decisions matter most. Stronger backbone models with lower intrinsic death rates may yield lower DAF values, revealing whether non-death routing signal emerges as the safety floor rises. Finally, environments with graded failure costs (rather than binary death) would test whether the dominance of catastrophic-failure avoidance extends to softer penalty structures.

file.content:
\section{Conclusion}

We introduced episode-level counterfactual analysis as a methodology for decomposing the routing signal in modular LLM agents into death-avoidance and non-death components. Applied to 245 ScienceWorld episodes across 11 task types with a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone, this analysis reveals that death avoidance accounts for approximately 90\% of routing value (DAF $= 90.41\%$ at $P{=}100$; $\Delta_\text{full} = 29.60$ vs.\ $\Delta_\text{nd} = 2.84$), with 78.9\% of non-tie labels arising from death asymmetry alone and strong cross-task correlation ($r = 0.97$, $p < 10^{-6}$).

Two lines of evidence support the generality of this finding. First, cross-environment analysis on MATH ($N{=}300$), where no death penalty exists, shows that the routing signal vanishes and directionally reverses: internal reasoning scores $+4.3$ percentage points higher than code execution ($81.0\%$ vs.\ $76.7\%$; CI $[0, 8.7]$, not significant), and the label distribution inverts from 86:9 deterministic-preferred in ScienceWorld to 30:17 internal-preferred. This contrast confirms that death avoidance, not an inherent advantage of deterministic computation, is the primary driver. Second, a Llama-3.1-8B pilot replicates the direction of the death differential (freeze death gap $+20\%$, consistent with Qwen's $+30\%$), providing preliminary evidence that the pattern generalizes across model families.

A trained routing classifier achieves only 57--59\% balanced accuracy across four seeds, confirming that once death avoidance is accounted for, the remaining learnable signal is thin. The classification head variant degenerates to always-deterministic predictions despite achieving non-trivial logit-level separation, suggesting that discriminative routing over LLM representations is fundamentally limited in this regime.

These results carry a practical implication: in environments with catastrophic failure modes, routing value is dominated by safety rather than efficiency. The router functions primarily as a safety critic---steering away from fatal actions---rather than as an optimizer selecting the more efficient strategy. System designers may therefore benefit from treating routing as a risk-management mechanism in such settings.

Several directions remain open. Step-level counterfactual labeling could localize where within an episode routing decisions matter most. Stronger backbone models with lower intrinsic death rates may yield lower DAF values, revealing whether non-death routing signal emerges as the safety floor rises. Finally, environments with graded failure costs (rather than binary death) would test whether the dominance of catastrophic-failure avoidance extends to softer penalty structures.

[写作进展] Patch — Seed Robustness 报告完成

## 修改清单

### 1. experiments.tex §4.3 Implicit Router 段落
- **旧**: "balanced accuracy is $58.1 \pm 0.8\%$"
- **新**: "Across four training seeds with a fixed data split, balanced accuracy is $57.6 \pm 0.5\%$; when the train/validation split is also varied, cross-split variance is substantially higher ($55.4 \pm 5.2\%$; Appendix E)"
- 数据源: plan-013-labeling-quality (fixed-split) + seed-robustness-core (cross-split)

### 2. 新增 Appendix E: Seed Robustness (main.tex)
- Per-seed breakdown 表格：fixed-split {42,123,456,789} vs cross-split {42,43,44,45}
- Balanced acc + Internal recall 双指标
- 10× variance 增幅说明 split sensitivity > training noise
- Bootstrap decomposition稳定性: DAF = 90.6%±4.2% (CI [81.6%, 98.8%]), r = 0.975±0.011 (CI [0.952, 0.995])

### 3. 更新 Appendix D: Router Training Details
- "57--59%" → "57--58%"（更精确反映 fixed-split range）
- 增加 cross-reference 到 Appendix E

### 4. 附带修复: conclusion.tex
- 移除 MATH 具体数字 (81.0/76.7/8.7)，改为引用 §5 Discussion

- `check_paper_consistency`: **0 critical**, 1 warning (dagger-2011 orphan — false positive, 实际在 main.tex Limitations 中引用)
- `paper_compile_and_check`: **PASS**, 0 critical warnings, 13 页

无。可提交 fresh review。

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".

- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.

[Director 指令] [Patch] Round 7 审稿修复 — EMNLP 2026 Main Conference, DDL 2026-05-25

收到 Round 7 fresh review，borderline reject。需要系统性修复 claim 强度和 scope 限定。以下是定稿的 Action Matrix，按优先级排列：

---

## Must-Fix（论文编辑部分）

**MF3: Scope qualifiers**
- Title 不变（"Death Avoidance as the Dominant Routing Signal" 无具体数字）
- Abstract 第一次提到 routing signal 时加限定："within completable-horizon tasks (11 of 30 ScienceWorld task types)"
- Conclusion 同步加 scope limitation

**MF4: Headline metric 重构**
- Abstract 以 78.9% death-asymmetry label fraction（penalty-independent）领衔
- DAF=~90% 降为 co-equal 指标，首次出现即标注 "at default penalty P=100"
- 全文所有 "90.41%" 改为 "~90%"
- Contributions list 中 DAF 描述附带 penalty-dependent caveat

**MF2: Contribution 4 降级**
- 从 "thin learnable signal" 改为 "preliminary observation"
